title: Little girl, arise (Mark 5:21–43)
hookLine: a father begs for his daughter, the news comes that she's dead, Jesus goes in anyway

cards: His name is Jairus. He's a leader of the synagogue, a respected man, the kind people come to for help. Today he's on his knees in the road.
His little daughter is dying. She's twelve. He begs Jesus: come, lay your hands on her, so she'll be healed and live.
Jesus goes with him. The crowd, the woman, the stopping, and every minute of that delay is a minute Jairus is counting. While Jesus is still speaking to the woman, men come from Jairus's house.
You can see their faces before they say it. Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the teacher any further?

teach.b: Mark says Jesus overheard, and turns to the father before the words can settle. In the Douay-Rheims: "Fear not, only believe." Four words, to a man who has just heard the worst news of his life.
Jesus takes only Peter, James and John, and goes to the house. It's full of mourners, weeping and wailing loudly, as people did. He says: why all this noise and weeping?
The girl is not dead, but sleeping. They laugh at him. They know dead when they see it.
He sends them all out and takes the parents and his three friends in to the girl.
He takes her by the hand and speaks to her in Aramaic, the everyday language of home, and Mark keeps the words: "Talitha cumi, which is, being interpreted: Damsel (I say to thee) arise."

teach.h: TALITHA CUMI — LITTLE GIRL, GET UP.
teach.b: Talitha: little girl. Cumi: get up. Words a parent might say on an ordinary morning.
She gets up and walks around. Mark says they were astonished. Then two tender details.
Jesus tells them to give her something to eat. And Mark gives her age, twelve, exactly how long the woman in the crowd had been bleeding.
Twelve years of illness, twelve years of life, both brought back on the same afternoon.

teach.h: DAMSEL, I SAY TO THEE, ARISE.
teach.b: Some readers think Mark wraps one story inside the other on purpose. Christians read this as one of the stories behind their hope in the resurrection: death spoken to like sleep, and a hand that says get up.

how: Catholics hear the raising of Jairus's daughter at Sunday Mass, and many parents pray for their children by name each day; the story is also read as a sign of hope in the resurrection.

games.q: you're Jairus. men from your house say your daughter is dead, and there's no need to trouble the teacher any further. what does Jesus say?
o: I'm sorry. go home to your family.
wait here while I finish with this crowd.
games.why: “Fear not, only believe.” and he goes to the house anyway, takes her hand and says: talitha cumi.

practice: Think of a child you know, a daughter, a son, a niece, a student, the kid next door, and ask what they're carrying right now: fear, sickness, a hard year at school, something you can't fix.
If you pray, hold them before God, the way Jairus knelt in the road; if you don't, hold them in your mind with love. Either way, let the two words sit with you: little girl, get up.

wordCard.voice: Little girl. Talitha in Aramaic, the word Jesus used when he took Jairus's daughter by the hand and told her to get up. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic, kept by Mark in Greek letters: little girl, get up. The Douay-Rheims spells it cumi.

carryVoice: Your line: fear not, only believe. Talitha cumi: little girl, get up. See you tomorrow, out on the water.
